title: Zacchaeus gives back
hook: a hated tax collector is welcomed, and gives back fourfold (Luke 19:1–10)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was accusers, who walked away one by one. Your line was put down the stone. Today, forgiveness from the other side: the one who did the wrong.

Jericho, and the streets are packed because Jesus is passing through. Somewhere at the back of the crowd is a rich man who can't see a thing. Luke gives us his name, Zacchaeus, his job, chief among the tax collectors, and one more detail: he was little of stature. So he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree to watch from the branches. Jesus reaches the spot, stops, looks up, and calls him by name.
screen: `A CROWD TOO TALL TO SEE OVER.` → `A RICH MAN UP A TREE.` → `CALLED BY NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the King James words, Jesus says: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." Not a lecture. Jesus invites himself to the man's house, and Zacchaeus comes down fast and receives him joyfully. Second, the grumbling. When people saw it, Luke says, they all murmured that he had gone to be a guest with a man that is a sinner. The welcome comes first, before any change, and the crowd doesn't like it. Third, the turn. Zacchaeus stands up and says: "Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." Fourfold. Not an apology alone, not just what he took. Four times over. Nobody demands this of him in the story. It pours out of him once he's been welcomed. Fourth, the answer. Jesus says: "This day is salvation come to this house," and adds, "the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." Some readers notice the order: the welcome came before the repair, and the repair was real and costly. Forgiveness, in this story, doesn't cancel making it right. It sets it free. And that closes the week: Tashlich, trespasses, Peter's question, the servant who forgot his forgiven talents, Father, forgive them, and a crowd putting down its stones. Zacchaeus adds the last piece: the one who has been welcomed gives back more than he took.
screen: `COME DOWN: TODAY, AT THY HOUSE.` · `THE CROWD MURMURS.` · `HALF TO THE POOR, FOURFOLD BACK.` · `WELCOME FIRST, THEN REPAIR.` · then, large: `I RESTORE HIM FOURFOLD.`

segments.voice: Turn the story around and find one old wrong you did, small enough to name and old enough that it's been quietly sitting there: a loan never repaid, a credit you took, a friend you dropped. Look at it squarely, without punishing yourself, and ask what giving it back would look like, a little more than even, until one concrete step comes to mind. If you pray, you can hold that step in your prayer.
Zacchaeus. The tax collector Jesus welcomed to dinner, who then promised half his goods to the poor and fourfold to anyone he had cheated. Today's word.
Your line: fourfold. The welcome came first, and the repair was real. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians read the story of Zacchaeus as a picture of welcome leading to repentance and restitution.

chat.says: Did Zacchaeus have to pay people back before Jesus would come to his house?
options: No. Jesus welcomed him first; then Zacchaeus chose to give back fourfold.
Yes. Jesus told him to repay everyone before he'd come into the house.
No, and once he was welcomed he no longer needed to repay anyone.
chat.meaning: Jesus invites himself to the house before any change. Nobody demands it, but Zacchaeus gives half to the poor and restores fourfold.
